title: Linear Probing Revisited: Tombstones Mark the Demise of Primary Clustering
venue: 2021 IEEE 62nd Annual Symposium on Foundations of Computer Science (FOCS)
verified_against: Crossref (DOI record, title 'Demise'); arXiv API 2107.01250 (arXiv title says 'Death'; published title is 'Demise'); full text of arXiv PDF skimmed (intro, results, technical overview)
solution: Shows that tombstones left by deletions create an anti-clustering effect in (ordered) linear probing, so amortized insertion cost at load 1-1/x is x polylog(x) rather than x^2. Also gives 'graveyard hashing', a linear-probing variant with periodic rebuilds that plants tombstones, achieving O(x) expected cost per operation on any operation sequence.
methodology:
Probabilistic analysis of ordered linear probing under insert/delete workloads with rebuild windows of size R. The analysis reduces insertion cost to crossing numbers of intervals, then through a chain of problem transformations to a combinatorial-geometry question about monotone lattice paths (path surplus) with blue/red dots.
The bound is shown tight for hovering workloads in the classical setting (O~(x^1.5) with an Omega(x^1.5 lg lg x) lower bound); a larger rebuild window R=n/polylog(x) gives O~(x). Graveyard hashing is analysed separately (the paper states it needs 5-independent hashing).
results: Amortized expected insertion cost x polylog(x) at load 1-1/x with queries O(x); graveyard hashing gives O(x) per operation and 1+o(1) block transfers when x=o(B), versus the B=Omega(x^2) needed earlier.
gap: (Our assessment) Analyses expected amortized time under random deletions with tombstones and rebuilds; it does not study LIFO (stack-ordered) deletions with exact undo, nor exact refusal probabilities for a hard probe limit.

title: Optimal Non-oblivious Open Addressing
venue: Proceedings of the 57th Annual ACM Symposium on Theory of Computing (STOC '25)
verified_against: Crossref (DOI record; STOC 2025, not 2023); arXiv API 2503.13628; arXiv PDF skimmed (abstract, intro)
solution: Constructs a non-oblivious open-addressed hash table ('partner hashing') with O(1)-time operations even when the table is completely full, including a dynamically resized version using exactly as many slots as elements. Time bounds hold with high probability using only O(1) O(1)-wise independent hash functions.
methodology: The main technique encodes metadata in the relative ordering of the stored elements, simulating a Theta(n log n)-bit RAM with O(log n)-bit words inside the permutation of elements, with O(1) access and efficient updates. The intro presents a warm-up structure first and then refinements for resizing and high-probability bounds (read at intro level only; proofs not read).
results: Constant-time insert/delete/query at load factor 1 (full table), with high probability; this bypasses the Omega(log log eps^-1) lower bound that holds for oblivious open addressing.
gap: (Our assessment) Gives up the simple structure of classical open addressing (probe sequence plus naive layout) by encoding data in element order; says nothing about plain linear probing with a probe limit, stack-ordered deletes, or exact refusal probabilities.

title: Optimal Bounds for Open Addressing Without Reordering
venue: 2024 IEEE 65th Annual Symposium on Foundations of Computer Science (FOCS)
verified_against: Crossref (DOI record); arXiv API 2501.02305; arXiv PDF skimmed (abstract, intro, Theorems 1-2)
solution: Gives 'elastic hashing', a non-greedy open-addressed table without reordering with O(1) amortized and O(log delta^-1) worst-case expected probe complexity, and 'funnel hashing', a greedy scheme with O(log^2 delta^-1) worst-case expected probes. This disproves Yao's 1985 conjecture that uniform probing is optimal among greedy schemes.
methodology: Constructions partition the array into geometrically organized sub-arrays (levels) so that insertions can probe far down the probe sequence before settling, bypassing the coupon-collector bottleneck. Matching lower bounds are proved: Omega(log delta^-1) for any non-reordering table, Omega(log^2 delta^-1) for greedy schemes, and Omega(log^2 delta^-1 + log log n) w.h.p. (details of proofs not read).
results: Insertion-only open addressing without reordering is solved up to constants: amortized O(1), worst-case expected O(log delta^-1); funnel hashing beats uniform probing's Theta(delta^-1) for greedy schemes, all with matching lower bounds.
gap: (Our assessment) Insertion-only model and delta-fraction slack; no deletions, no stack discipline, no hard probe cap with refusals, and the structures are far from the plain linear probing used in compiler symbol tables.

title: Tiny Pointers
venue: Proceedings of the 2023 Annual ACM-SIAM Symposium on Discrete Algorithms (SODA)
verified_against: Crossref (SODA 2023 chapter record; journal version ACM Trans. Algorithms 21(4), 2025, DOI 10.1145/3700594, also found); arXiv API 2111.12800
solution: Introduces tiny pointers: o(log n)-bit replacements for log n-bit pointers at constant-factor time overhead, with optimal fixed-size and variable-size constructions. Applies them to data retrieval, succinct dynamic BSTs, stable dictionaries, variable-size-key dictionaries and the stash problem.
methodology: Based on the abstract only: the constructions revisit classic balls-and-bins problems, and the tiny-pointer theory gives optimal sizes Theta(log log log n + log k) bits (fixed) and Theta(log k) expected bits (variable) at load 1-1/k. Technique details were not read beyond the abstract.
results: Optimal tiny-pointer sizes at load factor 1-1/k, and space-efficient solutions to five classic data-structure problems 'for free'.
gap: (Our assessment) Space-efficiency theory for pointer replacement; not about probe-limited linear probing, refusals, or LIFO deletion. Cite as background on space-time tradeoffs in hashing.

title: Iceberg Hashing: Optimizing Many Hash-Table Criteria at Once
verified_against: Crossref (journal record; page range given as 1-51, article number not shown); arXiv API 2109.04548; arXiv PDF abstract read
solution: Introduces Iceberg hashing, a stable hash table with constant-time operations, load factor up to 1-o(1), and strong space, cache and failure-probability guarantees. Adds 'waterfall addressing', an indirection-free resizing technique.
methodology: Based on the abstract only: uses the front-yard/backyard design paradigm, with new general-purpose techniques for stability and very-high-probability guarantees. Space bound matches the Demaine et al. lower bound for stable tables when keys are Theta(log n) bits.
results: Simultaneously best-known constant-time operations, space efficiency (log C(|U|,n) + O(n log log n) bits), cache efficiency and low failure probability, while being stable.
gap: (Our assessment) A multi-objective chaining/bucketing design for general dictionaries; it does not address plain linear probing under stack-ordered deletion or exact refusal probabilities.

title: Linear Probing with Non-Greedy Insertions
verified_against: arXiv API 2607.17494 (submitted 2026-07-20; v2 11 Sep 2026); arXiv PDF intro, theorem statements and lower-bound proof overview read. No journal/conference record found. NOTE: the paper introduces 'interlinear probing' inside; the title is not 'Interlinear probing'.
solution: Introduces interlinear probing, a non-greedy insertion rule for linear probing (an insertion may skip a free slot to leave it for later) with no reordering. Given x in advance, worst-case expected insertion and positive-query time is O(x log x) at load 1-1/x, versus Theta(x^2) for greedy linear probing.
methodology:
Upper bounds: a stable non-greedy variant of linear probing, extended with a new stopping rule so negative queries cost O(x log^2 x), and a further extension giving O(x) amortized insertion. Lower bound: a multiscale potential argument over power-of-two block sizes compares imbalance from random home locations with the final-placement imbalance, showing Omega(x sqrt(log x)) for any stable strategy.
Upper bounds assume x <= n^0.49 and x known in advance.
results: Optimal worst-case expected insertion time among stable linear-probing strategies is x (log x)^Theta(1): O(x log x) upper bound versus Omega(x sqrt(log x)) lower bound.
gap: (Our assessment) Insertion-only (and the 'no reordering' stable model) with expected time; no deletions, no hard probe cap with refusal probabilities, and no stack-ordered undo.

title: Locality in Open Addressing Hash Tables
verified_against: arXiv API 2607.16390 (submitted 2026-07-17); arXiv PDF abstract, results and overview read. No published venue found.
solution: Studies locality (distance from the first probe to the farthest cell inspected) of open addressing without reordering. Shows no scheme can have locality o(1/eps^2) at all loads simultaneously, which explains why linear probing is hard to beat on locality.
methodology:
Lower bound via a 'transport' statement: m=(1-eps)n random home locations from any distribution on a cycle need total movement Omega(n/eps) to reach distinct cells (proved first for uniform, then via convexity for any distribution), then converted to hashing bounds. Upper bounds use a multilevel construction for known load and a variance lemma Var(|O_t intersect S|) <= |S| for symmetric probing schemes, giving a load-oblivious greedy scheme with O(1/eps) probes and probe i at distance O(i^2).
The paper abstract on arXiv says locality-optimal known-load schemes have cost O~(1/eps).
results: Omega(1/eps^2) locality barrier at every load, Omega(1/eps) amortized locality lower bound even for known final load, and matching known-load upper bounds up to logs (the full-text theorem states O(log^3(1/eps)/eps)).
gap: (Our assessment) Insertion-only expected-cost bounds; no deletions, no stack discipline, and no exact distribution of refusals under a fixed probe cap.

title: Bounded Linear Probing Hashing
venue: 37th International Conference on Probabilistic, Combinatorial and Asymptotic Methods for the Analysis of Algorithms (AofA 2026), LIPIcs vol. 381
verified_against: Dagstuhl DROPS record (published 2026-07-13, LIPIcs vol. 381, article 28); PDF text read (abstract, intro, motivation, model, theorems 1-4, conclusion). Crossref returned no record for the DOI at query time. NOTE: this is not a Robin Hood paper; it analyses a probe-capped linear probing process.
read_level: full text except proofs (abstract, intro, model, theorem statements, conclusion)
solution: Introduces bounded linear probing: an insertion probes at most p consecutive cells and is discarded (counted as failed) if all are occupied. It interpolates between the coupon collector (p=1) and classical linear probing (p>=n). Derives the expected number of insertion attempts needed to fill the table.
methodology:
Analytic combinatorics: tables are grouped by circular symmetry (as in Knuth) into full and almost-full tables with a 'trash bin' of failed insertions. A non-linear PDE for the bivariate generating functions (Theorem 1 and 2) is derived using a full algebra of operators, then solved in closed form (Theorems 3 and 4).
Asymptotics of the expected filling time are obtained from the closed forms (Theorem 5), and compared to experiments. Motivated by long-message second-preimage attacks on Merkle-Damgard hash functions.
results: Closed-form generating functions for full and almost-full tables for any p, and the asymptotic expected number of insertion trials to fill a table, which decreases by almost a factor p as p grows.
gap: (Our assessment) Closest prior work on probe-limited linear probing, but insertion-only with discarded failures counted until the table is full; no deletions, no LIFO/exact-undo discipline, no exact refusal probability at fixed load. The paper itself lists success probability at a given fill ratio, variance and limit laws as open.

title: Interval and l-interval rational parking functions
verified_against: Crossref (DOI 10.46298/dmtcs.12598, issued 2024-11-04); arXiv API 2311.14055 (journal_ref confirms DMTCS vol. 26:1); arXiv PDF header and abstract read. Author names lightly ASCII-folded in this file (Tomas, Martinez Mori, Quinonez); Crossref has the accents.
solution: Generalizes interval parking functions to n cars and m>=n spots (interval rational parking functions) and counts them, then studies the subset where each car parks at most l spots from its preference (l-interval).
methodology: Enumerative combinatorics: a counting formula for interval rational parking functions, recursive formulas for l-interval ones, and nondecreasing l-interval counts via the outcome map; for l=1 a bijection with barred preferential arrangements. Beyond the abstract, details were not read.
results: Enumeration formulas (closed and recursive), a Fibonacci-type count for the intersection with Fubini rankings, and the l=1 bijection with barred preferential arrangements (recovering the unit-interval result of Hadaway and Harris).
gap: (Our assessment) The l-interval condition is a probe limit in parking-function language, but the paper counts configurations; it has no hashing interpretation, no deletion/undo, and no probability law for refusals with random keys.

title: Parking Functions: From Combinatorics to Probability
venue: Methodology and Computing in Applied Probability
verified_against: Crossref (DOI record, issued 2023-02-18, vol 25 issue 1, article number 32); arXiv API 2103.17180; arXiv PDF abstract and intro read
solution: Studies parking functions PF(m,n) with m cars and n spots (m<=n): bijections to spanning forests, the link to Tutte polynomials, and probabilistic properties of a uniform parking function, including the law of a single coordinate.
methodology: Bijective combinatorics between parking functions and rooted spanning forests with m cars and n spots, relating the displacement enumerator to the inversion enumerator of forests and to counts of labeled graphs. Probabilistic parts derive coordinate laws and a recurrence for the displacement enumerator, adapting known results on random linear probes to get the covariance of two coordinates when m=n.
results: Bijections PF(m,n) <-> forests F(n+1,n+1-m); displacement enumerator identity; formula for the law of a single coordinate; covariance between two coordinates when m=n.
gap: (Our assessment) Covers the full-success event (all cars park) and displacement; it does not give refusal probabilities under a probe limit with an arriving/departing (stack) discipline.

title: Interval parking functions
verified_against: Crossref (DOI record, issued 2021-02, vol 123, article 102129); arXiv API 2006.09321 (submitted 2020-06-16); arXiv PDF abstract and intro read
solution: Defines interval parking functions (each car accepts only an interval [a(i),b(i)] of spots) as pairs (a,b) of a parking function and a dual parking function, and studies which pairs of outcome permutations are reachable.
methodology: Order-theoretic combinatorics on the symmetric group: proves the transitive closure of reachability (pseudoreachability) equals the bubble-sorting order, expressed via du Cloux's normal form and related to Armstrong's sorting order. The count of IPFs for n cars is n!(n+1)^(n-1) (stated in the intro).
results: The pseudoreachability order is exactly the bubble-sorting order on S_n, isomorphic to a product of chains of lengths 2,...,n; counts of IPFs given.
gap: (Our assessment) Algebraic/order structure of outcomes for interval constraints; no probabilistic refusal law and no connection to hash-table deletion or stack discipline.

title: Tight Bounds for Classical Open Addressing
venue: 2024 IEEE 65th Annual Symposium on Foundations of Computer Science (FOCS)
verified_against: Crossref (DOI record); arXiv API 2409.11280; arXiv PDF abstract and intro read
solution: Introduces 'rainbow hashing', a classical (oblivious) open-addressed table at load 1-eps with O(1) expected queries and O(log log eps^-1) expected insertions and deletions, including a dynamically resized variant, and proves this tradeoff optimal.
methodology:
Rainbow hashing assigns 'colors' to elements to decide table layout. The lower bound Omega(log log eps^-1) for any classical open-addressed table with O(log log eps^-1)-time positive queries extends the potential-function technique (average log-probe complexity) of an earlier paper; it also applies to the number of items rearranged.
Proof details beyond the intro were not read.
results: Tight Theta(log log eps^-1) update time at load 1-eps with O(1) queries, resolving the optimal time complexity of oblivious open addressing; dynamic resizing costs nothing extra.
gap: (Our assessment) Asymptotic expected-time tradeoffs for general deletions; no exact finite-n laws, no LIFO deletion discipline, and no probe-capped refusal probability.

title: Tight Analyses of Ordered and Unordered Linear Probing
venue: 2024 IEEE 65th Annual Symposium on Foundations of Computer Science (FOCS)
verified_against: Crossref (DOI record, FOCS 2024); arXiv API 2501.11582 (submitted 2025-01-20); arXiv PDF abstract and intro read
solution: Settles the amortized insertion cost of linear probing with tombstones at load 1-1/x at Theta(x log^1.5 x), and extends the bounds from ordered linear probing to the classical unordered variant used in practice.
methodology: Reduces the problem to the path surplus problem (maximum over monotone grid paths of blue minus red Poisson dots) and gives a new analysis showing expected maximum surplus Theta(m log^0.75 m). A tighter reduction from path surplus back to ordered linear probing then yields matching bounds with an optimally chosen rebuild window.
results: Theta(x log^1.5 x) worst-case amortized insertion/deletion time with O(x) queries; path surplus Theta(m log^0.75 m).
gap: (Our assessment) Asymptotic amortized cost under random (not stack-ordered) deletes with rebuilds; no exact probabilities of refusal under a fixed probe limit.

title: Quadratic Probing Revisited: Smoothed Analysis and the Fall of Robin Hood
verified_against: arXiv API 2607.13247 (submitted 2026-07-14); arXiv PDF abstract and intro read. No published venue found.
solution: Analyses a smoothed variant of quadratic probing (each key's k-th probe is expected at offset Theta(k^2)) under Robin Hood and anti-Robin Hood orderings, and shows a separation: anti-Robin Hood gets Theta(log eps^-1) expected query time at load 1-eps, Robin Hood only Theta(eps^-1/2).
methodology:
Probabilistic analysis of insertion order policies in a model where offset j is included in a key's offset sequence independently with probability 1/sqrt(j). The analysis extends to degree-d probing (Theta(eps^-1/d) for Robin Hood), and a probabilistic-method argument shows almost every fixed-offset degree-d sequence achieves O(log eps^-1) under anti-Robin Hood.
Proof details beyond the intro were not read.
results: Robin Hood ordering equalizes but worsens query times for smoothed quadratic probing (Theta(eps^-1/2)); anti-Robin Hood matches the conjectured O(log eps^-1) for quadratic probing.
gap: (Our assessment) Relevant for the Robin Hood discussion, but it concerns non-linear probe sequences and expected query time at load 1-eps, not linear probing with a hard probe cap, deletions, or refusal probabilities.

title: On the optimal time/space tradeoff for hash tables
venue: Proceedings of the 54th Annual ACM SIGACT Symposium on Theory of Computing (STOC '22)
verified_against: Crossref (DOI record, STOC 2022); arXiv API 2111.00602; arXiv PDF abstract read
solution: Shows O(log log n) wasted bits per key is not optimal: for any k in [log* n], O(k)-time updates, O(1)-time queries and O(log^(k) n) wasted bits per key are achievable w.h.p., and this tradeoff is best possible for a large class of hash tables.
methodology: Based on the abstract only: constructive upper bounds for fixed-capacity and dynamically resized tables (including large keys), plus lower bounds for a class of tables built with the current framework for succinct constant-time hash tables. Technique details were not read.
results: Time/space tradeoff curve where each extra additive constant of update time reduces wasted bits per key exponentially; applies to dynamic resizing and yields a succinct dynamic filter.
gap: (Our assessment) Space-efficiency for general dictionaries; not about open addressing with probe caps, LIFO deletion, or exact refusal laws. Background only.
